newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asia stocks should get reprieve from Dow recovery.
newsitem.headline: Asia stocks should get reprieve from Dow recovery.

text.p: The majority of Asian stock markets should take their cue in the upcoming week from the latest twists and turns in U.S. stocks.
The Dow Jones industrials index closed up more than 100 points last Friday, which was the sixth sharpest rise in the history of the average and reversed nearly all the Dow's losses last week.
Wall Street had been hit earlier in the week by fresh U.S. inflation jitters, which in turn had taken its toll on holiday depleted Asia stock markets.

TOKYO - The Tokyo market will reopen on Monday, hoping to shrug off the glum tone of 1996. The Nikkei average of 225 leading shares ended Dec 30 at 19,361.35, about 500 points below its 1995 close, reflecting the shifting state of the Japanese economy and the fortune of the yen.
HONG KONG - The outlook for Hong Kong stocks in the coming week is mixed, but any downside looks limited particularly following Wall Street's recovery.
"It is possible we could see the index fall to the 13,000 level or slightly lower," said Michael Ng, dealing director at Sassoon Securities. "I am a little worried about the U.S. bond market."

The Hang Seng Index closed 19.35 points higher at 13,222.79 on Friday. Over the holiday-shortened week, the index shed 181.35 points or 1.35 percent. Turnover was particularly heavy, averaging HK$10.32 a day in the three full trading days last week.
BANGKOK - Thai stocks are expected to rebound in the upcoming week after heavy recent setbacks as bargain hunters seek out deeply discounted stocks, brokers said.

"The index has a good chance to rebound next week following bruising falls on Thursday and Friday. But the expected gains will be minimal on absence of positive factors in the market," said Somchai Trairattanapirom of SITCA Investment.
The SET index closed at 787.47 on Friday against 835.71 a week ago.
KUALA LUMPUR - Malaysian stocks are expected to firm next week as traders return from holidays and liquidity improves, but shares will follow closely U.S. market sentiment, brokers said.
Irene Tan, head of research at Vickers Ballas, said investors could return to business in a buying mood. "It should be more positive next week, with more activity," she said.
The Composite Index of 100 large-capitalised stocks rose 22.45 points this week to 1,231.45.
"What happens next week here depends on what happens in the U.S. market," said Matthew Geiger, head of research at Phileo Allied.
JAKARTA - Jakarta share prices are expected to remain steady in the coming week, with expected speculative buying of second-liners and blue chips buying, brokers said.
"Prices are likely to remain steady, with the government's recent decision to revise local telephone tariffs seen to sustain an upward trend in Telkom," one broker said.
Another broker said President Suharto's annual 1997-98 (April-March) budget speech scheduled for January 6, was also likely to have a strong impact on the market.
On Friday, the Jakarta composite index closed 8.09 points higher at 646.19 points, from last's week close of 637.43.
MANILA - The steep-rise of the Dow Jones on Friday and prospects of investors re-emerging from Christmas holidays should boost Philippine shares next week, analysts said.
"I expect the 101-point gain of the Dow Jones to elicit applause from market players," said Irving Ackerman, president at I. Ackerman and Co.
The composite index closed on Friday at 3,169.26 points, down 1.30 points from a week earlier close of 3,170.56.
KARACHI - Pakistani stocks are likely to remain mixed to weak next week mainly because of political uncertainty ahead of February 3 general elections, dealers said.
"The index is likely to move in a narrow band in thin volumes as political uncertainty has weakened sentiment," dealer Ali Asghar of Fortunes Securities said.
On Thursday, the Karachi 100-share index rose 1.26 percent to end at 1,370.33 compared to 1,375.55 a week earlier.
COLOMBO - Sri Lankan stocks, recovering in the new year after a poor performance in 1996, are not expected to respond immediately to the Dow's 100-plus point rally, brokers said.
"We don't expect it to have a major impact on our market," said Sanjeeva Gunewardena, manager institutional sales at Commercial Stock Brokers.
The all share, which began the year at the psychologically important 600-point barrier, closed up at 607.1 on Friday.
SEOUL - Seoul shares may be hit by strike fears at the start of the upcoming week after falling to a 45-month low on Saturday, brokers said.
"Labour unrest is expected to flare up again from Monday. That expectation prompted the sale of shares today," said Kim Heung-shik of Hyundai Securities.
On Saturday, the composite index closed at 643.41, compared with last Friday's closing of 651.22.
SINGAPORE - Dealers in Singapore said Wall Street's performance would be closely watched for near-term market direction given a lack of domestic factors.
"The market is looking to the U.S. for direction," said a dealer with a local institution.
Dealers said activity would improve next week with most fund managers opening their books for the New Year.
The key Straits Times Industrials Index ended up 7.29 points at 2,224.08 on Friday, against 2,202.60 on December 27.
SYDNEY - Australian shares were seen mixed in the near term as traders cast a nervous eye over see-sawing U.S. markets.
The All Ordinaries index closed at 2,399.5, up 3.9 points over the week after touching record highs and closes of 2,426.5 and 2,424.6 respectively on the last day of 1996.
"The market primarily looks to the U.S. for a lead, be it positive or otherwise, and that's not going to change too much for a while," said Andrew Sekely, head of equities at Intersuisse Ltd.

TAIPEI - Taiwan share prices may be hit by continued political worries after the market was hit on Saturday by concern over the recent resignation of Taiwan provincial governor James Soong, said brokers.
Soong resigned on Tuesday in a widening constitutional row over plans by the island's exiled Republic of China government to dismantle his administration in the name of efficiency.
The index ended down 113.59 points, or 1.64 percent, to 6,820.35, off a low of 6,789.34.
